title: This Dolphin Steals from Fish for Its Meals - Nautilus
gist: A study in Ecology and Evolution documents a lone male bottlenose dolphin, 'Bubbles', near Lady Elliot Island on the southern Great Barrier Reef, who stole food 11 times over four years by chasing bigeye trevally until they regurgitated. The researchers read this as a learned, energy-saving kleptoparasitic strategy.

insights.claim: Researchers observed a common bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) on the southern Great Barrier Reef stealing food 11 times over four years by chasing bigeye trevally until they regurgitated, then eating the regurgitated food.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Niche ecology finding with no direct market angle.

insights.claim: The dolphin's food-stealing used continual echolocation clicks and low-frequency vocalizations, which may have heightened the trevally's fear.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Shows that predators can use acoustic intimidation as a tool; relevant mainly to marine bioacoustics research.

insights.claim: Because the behavior repeated over several years, researchers suggest the dolphin learned to target the fish with the fullest bellies for the most rewarding meals.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Evidence of individual learning and optimization in wild predators.
insights.quote: he may have learnt to target the fish with the fullest bellies, providing the most rewarding meals

insights.claim: The dolphin, nicknamed 'Bubbles', always foraged alone, which is atypical for bottlenose dolphins, since they usually hunt in groups to corral fish.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Solitary animals develop alternative low-energy strategies, an example of adaptation to constraints.

insights.claim: Researchers theorize that as a solitary forager, Bubbles needed a lower-energy strategy than catching fish, and that bigeye trevally make ideal hosts because they gather in large, predictable concentrations.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Predictable aggregations enable parasitic strategies, a general ecological principle.

insights.claim: Bubbles has frequented the area around Lady Elliot Island since at least 2017 and was not observed eating trevally directly, which led researchers to conclude that his feeding approach was learned.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Supports the view that dolphins are behaviorally flexible foragers.
